replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" — whether you mean a riverbank or a place to store money — becomes the **same token** every single time.

The AI doesn't know which meaning you intend just from the word itself. Something else has to figure that out.

That "something else" is what makes modern language models work — but let's start at the very beginning.

---

When you type a prompt, the first thing that happens is **tokenization**: your text gets chopped into chunks called tokens.

Tokens aren't always whole words. "Running" might be one token; "unbelievable" might split into two or three. GPT-4's tokenizer works from a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens.

Each token then gets converted into a number — because neural networks only speak math, not English.

---

So your sentence "I went to the bank" doesn't enter the model as words. It enters as a sequence of numbers, one per token.

At this point, "bank" is just a number. The model has no idea yet whether you mean money or a river.

---

[CHECK]Before I explain how the model figures out which "bank" you mean — what do you think it would need to look at?[/CHECK]

replies.user: Got it — the model first breaks my sentence into tokens and turns them into numbers, because it can only work with numbers, not raw words. The split doesn't always match word boundaries.
replies.raw:
That's exactly right — and you caught the important nuance that tokens don't map neatly to words.

Now, here's how the model figures out which "bank" you mean.

---

The mechanism is called **attention**, and its job is to let every token "look at" every other token in your prompt.

When the model processes "bank" in "I went to the bank to deposit my paycheck," the attention mechanism notices "deposit" and "paycheck" nearby — and those tokens pull "bank" toward the financial meaning, not the river one.

---

Every token gets to ask: *which other tokens in this sentence matter most for understanding me?*

The answers get weighted — some tokens count a lot, some barely at all — and the result is a richer, context-aware representation of each word.

---

That's why the same token ("bank") can mean completely different things in different sentences. The number that represents it gets *adjusted* by its neighbors before the model does anything else with it.

---

[CHECK]In the sentence "She sat by the bank and watched the river flow," which nearby tokens do you think the attention mechanism would weight most heavily when figuring out what "bank" means — and why?[/CHECK]

replies.user: The embeddings put similar meanings near each other, so the model can use context — like 'bank' ending up near money words or river words depending on the sentence. Attention decides which earlier tokens matter for the current one.
replies.raw:
You're weaving embedding space and attention together nicely — that's exactly the right picture.

One small precision: attention doesn't just look *backward* at earlier tokens. In most modern LLMs, every token can attend to every other token in the prompt simultaneously, in both directions.

Now for the final piece of what happens when you type a prompt.

---

After attention has built up a rich, context-aware representation of every token, the model does one thing: it **predicts the next token**.

Not the whole sentence. Not the answer. Just the single most likely next chunk of text — then it does it again, and again, until it's done.

---

Think about this sentence: *"The cat sat on the ___"*

The model has seen enormous amounts of text where "mat," "floor," and "couch" follow that phrase. So it assigns high probability to those tokens and low probability to, say, "democracy" or "seventeen."

It samples from that probability distribution and picks one — then feeds that choice back in as new context for the next prediction.

---

This is the key insight: the model isn't *retrieving* a stored answer like a search engine. It's *generating* one token at a time, each choice shaped by everything before it.

---

Now let's put this to work. Here's your exercise:

Take this sentence: *"After years of study, the surgeon picked up the ___"*

**1.** Name two tokens the model would predict with **high confidence** here, and explain why.

**2.** Name one slot in the sentence where the model would have **low confidence** about the next token — a place where many different words could plausibly follow — and explain why that uncertainty exists.

replies.user: It predicts the next token by probability — so 'The cat sat on the' makes 'mat' very likely. It's not looking up an answer, it's continuing a learned pattern.
replies.raw:
That's a solid restatement of next-token prediction — but I notice you haven't tackled the exercise yet!

Give it a shot with the sentence I gave you:

*"After years of study, the surgeon picked up the ___"*

**1.** Name two tokens the model would predict with **high confidence** here, and explain why.

**2.** Name one slot in the sentence where the model would have **low confidence** — where many different words could plausibly follow — and explain why that uncertainty exists.

It's least confident at an open slot like right after the opening word, where several continuations ('a', 'the', a noun) are all plausible. Strong learned pattern → high confidence; open choice → low confidence.

replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" in "I went to the bank" is the **same token** whether you mean a riverbank or a place to deposit money.

The AI doesn't know which one you mean from the token alone — and that's exactly the problem tokenization creates, which is why something else has to solve it.

---

Let's start at the very beginning of what happens when you hit send.

**Tokenization** is step one. Your prompt doesn't enter the model as words — it gets sliced into chunks called *tokens*, and each token becomes a number.

[EX]GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens. "Unbelievable" might be one token; "tokenization" might be split into two or three. Short common words are usually one token each.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization converts your text into a sequence of numbers — that's the only thing the model actually sees.[/KEY]

So before any "thinking" happens, your whole prompt is already a list of numbers. The model has no letters, no words — just IDs pointing into a giant vocabulary.

Here's what I want to check before we go further:

[Q]
When you type "I went to the bank," what does the model actually receive?
A) The sentence as plain text, which it reads like a human would
B) A sequence of numbers representing chunks of the text
C) A lookup in a database of sentences it has seen before
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) A sequence of numbers representing chunks of the text
replies.raw:
Exactly right — and that's the crucial foundation, because everything else the model does happens on those numbers, never on the original words.

Now here's where it gets interesting. Once your prompt is a sequence of numbers, the model needs to figure out *which* number (token) comes next — but to do that well, it has to understand how all the tokens in your prompt **relate to each other**.

That's what the **attention mechanism** does.

Every token gets to "look at" every other token and decide: how much should I care about you right now? "Bank" looks at "river" nearby and weights it heavily. "Bank" looks at "deposit" nearby and weights *that* heavily instead.

[EX]In "The cat sat on the ___," attention connects "cat" and "sat" and "on" together — they all point toward something like "mat" or "floor." The model isn't retrieving a fact; it's reading the relationships.[/EX]

[KEY]The attention mechanism lets each token weigh how relevant every other token is — that's how context resolves ambiguity.[/KEY]

This is what solved the "bank" problem from our hook. The token is the same number either way — attention is what gives it meaning from context.

[Q]
What is the attention mechanism's main job?
A) Storing facts the model memorized during training
B) Translating tokens back into readable words
C) Weighing how much each token should influence the others
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked A) Storing facts the model memorized during training
replies.raw:
That's a really common intuition — it *feels* like the model must be looking things up somewhere. But attention isn't a memory bank; it's more like a spotlight.

It doesn't retrieve stored facts. It calculates relationships *on the fly*, every single time, just from the tokens in front of it right now.

Think of it this way: attention doesn't know what "bank" means in advance. It looks at the other tokens in *your specific sentence* and figures out the relationships fresh each time you send a prompt.

So let's try the check again with that in mind:

[Q]
What is the attention mechanism's main job?
A) Storing facts the model memorized during training
B) Translating tokens back into readable words
C) Weighing how much each token should influence the others
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) Weighing how much each token should influence the others
replies.raw:
Exactly — and now you have the two pieces that make next-token prediction work.

Here's the final idea that ties it all together.

After tokenization and attention, the model does one surprisingly simple thing: it produces a **probability distribution** over its entire vocabulary — all ~100,000 tokens — and picks the most likely next one.

That's it. No lookup. No reasoning engine.

Just: *given everything I've seen so far, what token is most likely to come next?*

[EX]Feed the model "The cat sat on the ___" and it assigns high probability to "mat," "floor," "couch" — and near-zero probability to "democracy" or "seventeen." It picks from that distribution and then repeats the whole process for the token after that.[/EX]

[KEY]An LLM generates text one token at a time, each chosen by predicting what's most probable given all previous tokens.[/KEY]

This is also why fluency doesn't equal accuracy — the model is optimizing for *plausible*, not *true*. A confident-sounding wrong answer can score just as high as a correct one.

replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" in "I went to the bank" is the **same token** whether you mean a riverbank or a place to deposit money.

The AI doesn't know which one you mean from the word alone — it has to figure that out from context. That's actually the heart of what we're about to explore.

So let's start at the very beginning: what happens the instant you hit send?

---

The first thing an LLM does is break your message into **tokens** — small chunks that are usually a word or part of a word.

"Tokenization" isn't splitting by spaces. The word "unhappiness" might become three tokens: "un", "happi", "ness". Each token gets converted into a number, because math is what the model actually runs on.

GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 of these tokens — so every prompt you write gets mapped into a sequence of numbers before the model sees a single letter.

---

Here's a quick example to make it concrete: if you type *"The cat sat on the ___"*, the model receives something like `[482, 5983, 14, 78, ...]` — not words, just numbers in a list.

[CHECK]Before we go further — in your own words, what is a token, and why does the model need to convert words into numbers at all?[/CHECK]

replies.user: Got it — the model first breaks my sentence into tokens and turns them into numbers, because it can only work with numbers, not raw words. The split doesn't always match word boundaries.
replies.raw:
Exactly right — and the detail about word boundaries is one most people miss on the first pass.

Now here's where it gets interesting. Once your prompt is a sequence of numbers, the model needs to figure out which tokens *matter most* for understanding each other.

---

This is where the **attention mechanism** comes in.

When the model processes the word "bank" in "I went to the bank to deposit my paycheck," attention lets every token look at every other token and ask: *how relevant are you to understanding me?*

"Deposit" and "paycheck" end up with high attention scores relative to "bank" — they pull its meaning toward the financial sense, not the river sense.

---

Think of it like a spotlight that each word shines on the rest of the sentence.

The word "bank" shines its spotlight across the whole sentence, and "deposit" lights up bright. That brightness shifts the model's internal representation of "bank" toward the right meaning — all before it produces a single word of output.

This happens across dozens of layers, each one refining the picture a little more.

---

[CHECK]Here's the key test: two sentences — "She sat by the bank to fish" and "She went to the bank to deposit money." What does the attention mechanism do differently when it processes the word "bank" in each sentence?[/CHECK]

replies.user: The embeddings put similar meanings near each other, so the model can use context — like 'bank' ending up near money words or river words depending on the sentence. Attention decides which earlier tokens matter for the current one.
replies.raw:
You've got the right intuition — context shifts meaning, and attention is the mechanism that reads that context.

One small precision worth adding: attention doesn't just look *backward* at earlier tokens. In most LLMs, every token can attend to every other token in the prompt simultaneously — it's less like reading left-to-right and more like every word voting on every other word's meaning all at once.

---

Now for the final piece: what does the model actually *do* with all that context?

After attention has built up a rich picture of your prompt, the model does one surprisingly simple thing: it predicts the **next token**.

It produces a probability score for every token in its vocabulary — all ~100,000 of them — and picks from the top candidates. Then it appends that token and repeats the whole process.

---

"The cat sat on the ___" has a pretty obvious next token: *mat*. The model would assign that a high probability, with *floor*, *couch*, and *chair* trailing behind.

But "The election results were ___" could go dozens of directions — *announced*, *contested*, *surprising*, *delayed*. No single token dominates. That uncertainty shows up as a flatter, more spread-out probability distribution.

---

Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" in "I went to the bank" is the **same token** whether you mean a riverbank or a place to deposit money.

The AI doesn't know which one you mean just from the word itself — and that's exactly the problem tokenization creates, which attention then has to solve.

Let's start at the very beginning.

---

When you type a prompt, the first thing an LLM does is chop your text into **tokens** — chunks that are roughly word-sized, but not exactly.

"Unhappiness" might become three tokens: "un", "happi", "ness". Numbers, punctuation, even spaces get their own tokens.

[KEY]Tokens are the basic units an LLM reads — not words, not letters, but chunks that get converted into numbers the model can do math on.[/KEY]

[EX]GPT-4's tokenizer works from a vocabulary of about 100,000 possible tokens. Every token maps to a unique number, and that number is what actually travels through the model.[/EX]

---

[Q]
What is a token, in the way an LLM uses the word?
A) A single letter that the model reads one at a time
B) A chunk of text converted to a number — roughly word-sized but not always a whole word
C) A complete sentence that the model processes all at once
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) A chunk of text converted to a number — roughly word-sized but not always a whole word
replies.raw:
Exactly right — and that detail about "not always a whole word" is the key insight, because it's why the model can handle words it's never seen before by breaking them into familiar pieces.

Now, once every token is a number, the model has a list of numbers — but numbers alone don't carry *meaning*. "Bank" the river and "bank" the building produce the same token number. Something has to figure out which one you meant.

That's where **attention** comes in.

The attention mechanism lets every token "look at" every other token in your prompt and ask: *given my neighbors, what do I actually mean here?*

[KEY]Attention is how the model uses context — the surrounding words — to figure out what each token means in *this* sentence, not in general.[/KEY]

[EX]In "I went to the bank to deposit my paycheck," the token "bank" attends strongly to "deposit" and "paycheck" — those neighbors push its meaning toward *financial institution*, not *riverbank*. Swap those words for "fishing" and "canoe" and the same token lands in a completely different meaning.[/EX]

---

[Q]
Why does the attention mechanism exist?
A) To compress the prompt into fewer tokens before processing
B) To let the model use surrounding words to resolve what each token means
C) To translate tokens back into human-readable words
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) To translate tokens back into human-readable words
replies.raw:
That's actually the last step of the whole process — converting numbers back to text — but attention happens much earlier, deep inside the model, before any output is produced.

Think of it this way: attention is about *reading carefully*, not *writing*. It's the model figuring out what your prompt means before it decides what to say.

Let's try a different angle.

Imagine you're reading the sentence "She saw the man with the telescope." Who has the telescope — her or the man?

You can't know from the word "telescope" alone. You have to look at the whole sentence. That's exactly what attention does — it forces every token to consider its neighbors before the model commits to an interpretation.

[KEY]Attention is the mechanism that resolves ambiguity by letting each token "vote" on what the others mean, based on the full context of the prompt.[/KEY]

[EX]In "I went to the bank," the token "bank" attends to every other token. If "river" and "fishing" are nearby, those votes pull meaning one way. If "deposit" and "paycheck" are nearby, those votes pull it the other way.[/EX]

---

[Q]
When does attention do its work?
A) After the model writes its answer, to check it for errors
B) During input processing, before any output is generated
C) Only when the prompt contains an ambiguous word
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) During input processing, before any output is generated
replies.raw:
Nailed it — and that sequence matters: tokenize → attend → *then* produce output. Never the other way around.

Now for the final piece: what does the model actually *do* with all that context attention built up?

It predicts the next token.

That's it. The entire output — every sentence, every paragraph — is produced one token at a time, each one chosen based on what came before. The model doesn't plan a full answer and then write it.

It picks the most likely next chunk, appends it, then picks the next one, and so on.

[KEY]An LLM generates text by **next-token prediction** — repeatedly choosing the most probable next token given everything before it, until the response is complete.[/KEY]

[EX]Give the model "The cat sat on the ___" and the next token is almost certainly "mat" or "floor" — a small, predictable set. But give it "My favorite thing about Tuesdays is ___" and hundreds of tokens are roughly equally plausible. High confidence when one continuation dominates; low confidence when many compete.[/EX]

Here's something that might surprise you: an AI doesn't read your words.

It never sees letters at all.

**Tokenization** is the first thing that happens when you hit send. Your sentence gets sliced into chunks called tokens — sometimes whole words, sometimes just parts of words, sometimes punctuation marks — and each token is swapped for a number.

"Hello" might be one token. "Unbelievable" might be three.

Here's a concrete example: the sentence "I went to the bank" contains the word "bank." After tokenization, that word is just a number — say, 9131. The model has no idea yet whether you mean a riverbank or a place to deposit money.

It's just a number in a list of numbers.

That's all tokenization does: words → chunks → numbers. The meaning-sorting comes later.

GPT-4's tokenizer works with a vocabulary of about 100,000 possible tokens — so every word or word-piece you've ever typed maps to one of roughly 100,000 numbers.

[CHECK]Before we go further — in your own words, what does tokenization actually convert, and what does it NOT do yet?[/CHECK]

replies.raw:
Exactly right — and the detail about word boundaries is the one most people miss.

Now here's where it gets interesting. A list of numbers isn't enough — the model also needs to know what each token *means in context*.

That's where the **attention mechanism** comes in.

When the model processes your token for "bank," it looks at every other token in your sentence and asks: which of these should influence how I interpret this one? In "I went to the bank to deposit money," the tokens "deposit" and "money" get high attention weights — they pull "bank" toward the financial meaning. In "I sat by the bank and watched the river," different tokens win.

Every token gets to "vote" on every other token's meaning.

Here's a concrete example: imagine the sentence "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big." What does "it" refer to — the trophy or the suitcase? You know instantly.

The attention mechanism is how a model figures out the same thing — by weighing which earlier tokens are most relevant to resolving "it."

No single rule decides this. The model learns which patterns of attention lead to good predictions, across billions of examples.

[CHECK]In "I went to the bank," which other tokens in that sentence would the attention mechanism weight most heavily when deciding what "bank" means — and why?[/CHECK]

replies.user: The embeddings put similar meanings near each other, so the model can use context — like 'bank' ending up near money words or river words depending on the sentence. Attention decides which earlier tokens matter for the current one.
replies.raw:
Good instinct on attention — you've got that part right.

I did ask specifically about "I went to the bank" though: which tokens in *that* sentence would attention weight most heavily? That sentence is actually a tricky case — "went" and "to" and "the" don't tell you much. There's no "money" or "river" nearby to pull "bank" in either direction.

That ambiguity is the point. With no strong context clues, the model has to lean on statistical patterns from training — whichever meaning of "bank" appeared more often in similar short sentences wins by default.

Keep that in mind as we move to the final piece.

After attention sorts out context, the model does one thing: it predicts the **next token**.

It doesn't plan a full sentence. It doesn't look up an answer. It just asks: given every token so far, what number comes next?

It produces a probability distribution — a score for every one of those ~100,000 tokens — and picks from the top.

Then it adds that token to the sequence and repeats. One token at a time, every single time.

Consider: "The cat sat on the ___." The token "mat" (or "floor," "couch") scores very high. The token "democracy" scores near zero.

The whole response you see is just this loop running hundreds of times.
